drafts.subject: Re: Prospective GSoC contributor - where to start?
drafts.message:
Hi Fatima!

Thanks so much for reaching out — it's great to hear you're interested in contributing to Jaseci ahead of GSoC! A strong Python background and some familiarity with Jac is a fantastic foundation, so you're already off to a great start.

Here are some pointers to help you get going:

**Repositories to explore:**
- **jaseci** (github.com/Jaseci-Labs/jaseci) — the core engine. A good place to understand how the runtime, walkers, and nodes work under the hood.
- **jaseci-ai-kit** (github.com/Jaseci-Labs/jaseci_ai_kit) — a collection of AI/ML modules built on top of Jaseci. If you're interested in AI use cases, this is a great repo to contribute to and it's fairly approachable for newcomers.
- **jaseci-js** and **jaseci-ui** — front-end related repos if you're also interested in the web/UI side of things.

**Good first issues:**
Head to the Issues tab on any of those repos and filter by the `good first issue` and `help wanted` labels. Those are specifically tagged for newcomers and tend to be well-scoped. If you find one that looks interesting but you're not sure where to begin, don't hesitate to ask in the comments — mentors are happy to help you get unstuck.

**Next steps to deepen your familiarity:**
- Try building a small Jac program end-to-end (e.g., a simple graph traversal or a mini AI app using jaseci-ai-kit). Getting something running locally will help you understand the architecture much faster than just reading code.
- Skim the core `jaseci` repo's codebase, focusing on the walker and graph abstractions. Understanding how walkers traverse nodes/edges is central to everything in Jaseci.
- Once you've got your bearings, pick a good first issue and open a draft PR early — even if it's not complete, mentors can guide you.

**GSoC timeline & prerequisites:**
GSoC typically opens org applications in February, with contributor applications opening in March/April and coding running May–August. I'd recommend checking the official GSoC site (summerofcode.withgoogle.com) for exact dates as they're announced. For prerequisites, we generally look for contributors who've already engaged with the community and submitted at least one or two PRs before the application period — so starting now is exactly the right move! Having a merged contribution or two strengthens your proposal significantly.

**Community channels:**
- Join our Slack workspace (you can find the invite link on the Jaseci GitHub org page or at jaseci.org) — that's where most day-to-day discussion happens and where mentors are most active.
- You can also reach us at this email (impact@jaseci.org) anytime.
- Watch/star the repos you're interested in so you stay in the loop on discussions and new issues.

We're really glad you reached out early, Fatima. Jump into Slack, introduce yourself, and feel free to tag us once you've picked an issue to work on. Looking forward to having you in the community!

Best,
The Jaseci Team

drafts.subject: Re: Bug: edge traversal returns duplicates after node delete (repro attached)
drafts.message:
Hi Omar,

Thanks for the detailed repro — really appreciate the clear write-up and the offer to contribute.

**Is this a known issue?**
Yes, this is a known class of issue in Jaseci/Jac. When a node is destroyed, the graph engine doesn't always fully clean up dangling edge references on the neighboring nodes' edge lists. So [-->] traversal from a former neighbor can return stale/duplicate edge entries pointing to edges that were logically removed when the node was deleted. Your repro (A->B->C, delete B, traverse from A) is a solid minimal case that exposes it.

**Workaround you can ship now:**
A couple of options while a permanent fix lands:
1. **Filter stale edges post-traversal** — after calling [-->], filter the returned edges to drop any whose target node no longer exists (e.g., check `edge.target` validity or wrap in a guard). This is the safest drop-in fix and avoids touching your graph mutation logic.
2. **Explicit edge cleanup before node delete** — before destroying node B, explicitly disconnect/remove its incoming and outgoing edges from the neighbor nodes first, then delete the node. This keeps the edge lists consistent.

Option 1 is the least invasive for a production patch; option 2 is cleaner if you control the deletion path.

**GitHub issue:**
Yes, please do file one — it would be genuinely helpful. The repro snippet you described (create A, B, C; edges A->B, B->C; delete B; [-->] from A returns two stale edges) is exactly the kind of minimal repro that helps us pin it down quickly. If you can include the Jac version (0.10.2), the snippet, and the expected vs. actual output, that's ideal.

We'll track the fix against the issue and update the thread there as it progresses.

Thanks again for reporting this cleanly — it makes a real difference.

Best,
Jaseci Team

drafts.subject: Re: Press: quote on agentic programming languages (deadline Aug 5 EOD)
drafts.message:
Hi Grace,

Thanks for reaching out — happy to contribute to your piece. Here's a quote you can use, attributed to Jaseci:

"General-purpose programming languages were built for deterministic computation, not for autonomous, adaptive agents that must reason, coordinate, and act in dynamic environments. They leave developers to hand-stitch together the scaffolding — memory, orchestration, tool use, multi-agent coordination — that agentic software fundamentally requires, resulting in brittle and overly complex systems. Agent-native languages like Jaseci bake these primitives in at the language level, letting developers focus on behavior and outcomes rather than reinventing the plumbing with every project."

Let me know if you'd like a shorter version or any adjustments. Good luck with the article!

Best,
The Jaseci Team
impact@jaseci.org
